extracted.intended_audience: journalists (especially health and science reporters) looking to vet research and detect predatory journals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and checklists for journalists to identify and avoid predatory academic journals when reporting on research, including red flags, verification steps, and trusted indexing/membership signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop sources who can help you vet research studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop sources who can help you vet research studies. Speak with a statistician or biostatistician to check the data and methods of a research study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check resources like your local university, SciLine or the American Statistical Association for expert help in assessing methods and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check established lists and tools (with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Check lists such as the Retraction Watch Hijacked Journal Checker, Cabells and Beall’s List.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lists and tools can help find hijacked or questionable journals, but have limits: Beall’s List was criticized as subjective and opaque; Cabells is paywalled. Use such lists as one input among many and verify findings with other signals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask authors what other journals they tried to publish in
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask the authors of the study you’re covering what other journals they’ve tried to publish their research in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors tried several journals and were rejected but the paper appears in an unfamiliar journal, it doesn't prove the journal is predatory but can indicate how rigorous peer review may have been.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the business of academic publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a basic understanding of how the business of academic journal publishing works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding incentive structures (e.g., open-access fees, publisher revenue models) helps journalists spot motivations that may produce deceptive practices and prevents taking claims at face value.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or misleading information
rubrics_metrics.description: A predatory journal’s website or e-mails often present contradictory statements, fake impact factors, incorrect addresses, misrepresentations of the editorial board, false claims of indexing or membership of associations and misleading claims about the rigor of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for inconsistencies across a journal’s site and communications; verify claimed impact factors, editorial board members, and indexing with independent sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deviation from best editorial and publication practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Not following best editorial and publication practices set forth by DOAJ, OASPA, COPE, and WAME.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning signs should be assessed with care: journals are not eligible for DOAJ/COPE until after one year, and resource-limited legitimate journals may have unprofessional websites. Some journals may claim adherence but do not follow the practices—verify claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of transparency about editorial procedures and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of transparency regarding operational procedures like how editorial decisions are made and peer review is organized, and failure to provide contact information or details about article processing charges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reputable journal should clearly describe peer review workflows, editorial governance, contact details, and what (if any) fees will be charged and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertising an unrealistically short timeline for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising an unrealistically short timeline for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very fast promised turnarounds (e.g., acceptance within days) are a red flag for inadequate or nonexistent peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor copyediting and numerous grammatical errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing articles that have many grammatical errors with little or no copyediting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistently low editorial standards across published articles suggest weak editorial oversight and potential predatory behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hijacking journal names / creating illegitimate clones
rubrics_metrics.description: Hijacking the names of established and reputable journals and creating illegitimate clones that can appear higher in search results than the original journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tools like Retraction Watch’s Hijacked Journal Checker and cross-check ISSN and publisher details to detect clones or impostor titles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requiring authors to sign away copyright at submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring authors to sign away their copyright to the article at the time of submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious if a journal asks authors to transfer copyright before peer review or provides unclear or overly aggressive copyright terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressive and indiscriminate solicitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggressive solicitation, such as repeated e-mails to researchers. The solicitations are indiscriminate; many times, the invitee's expertise is outside the journal's scope. The emails tend to be excessively flattering and include bad formatting, spelling and grammar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated flattering invitations, poor email quality, and scope mismatches are signs of predatory outreach rather than targeted legitimate invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge of the journal (Think. Check. Submit items)
rubrics_metrics.description: Have you read any articles in the journal before? Is it easy to discover the latest papers in the journal? Is the name of the journal unique, and not the same or easily confused with another journal? Can you cross-check with information about the journal in the ISSN portal?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether the journal’s content is discoverable, whether its title is distinct (not easily confused with other journals), and verify ISSN details to distinguish legitimate titles from impostors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher’s contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the publisher’s name clearly displayed on the journal website?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A legitimate journal should prominently list a verifiable publisher name, physical address and methods to contact editorial staff; absence or vagueness is a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity about the journal’s peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the journal clear about its peer review process?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for specific descriptions (e.g., single-blind, double-blind, editorial review steps, timelines); vague or missing explanations suggest poor editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees for authors (APCs and financial transparency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the publisher explain on their website how they are financially supported? Does the journal site explain what its fees are for and when they will be charged?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent journals disclose article processing charges, when fees are assessed, and what fees cover; hidden or surprise fees are a red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for authors and conflict-of-interest policies
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the publisher have a clear policy regarding potential conflicts of interest for authors, editors and reviewers?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for author guidelines, COI policies, retraction and corrections policies—absence indicates weak governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher membership in recognized industry initiatives and trustworthy indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the journal a current member of the Committee on Publication Ethics and follow its guidelines? If the journal is open access, is it listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals? If the publisher offers an open access option, is it a current member of the Open Access Scholarly Publishers’ Association? Is the journal hosted on regional trusted platforms (Journals Online, AJOL) or indexed in Scielo, Latindex, Redalyc, Web of Science, etc.?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Memberships and indexing provide signals of trustworthiness; verify listings directly with the index or organisation rather than trusting claims on the journal website.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer verifying indexing/memberships over relying solely on 'predatory' lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of looking at lists of 'predatory journals,' journalists should look to see if journals are indexed in lists that suggest trustworthiness, like OASPA, Web of Science, Redalyc, Scielo, Latindex, etc., and whether they are members of COPE and adhere to its guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indexing/membership in reputable services is a stronger positive signal than binary inclusion on a 'predatory' list; always cross-check with the index/association directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits and debate around the term 'predatory journals'
rubrics_metrics.description: The binary label 'predatory' is seen as overly simplistic and some critics argue established journals with high fees or aggressive commercial behaviour might also behave problematically; some high-quality research can appear in questionable journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess warning signs with nuance—consider context (regional journals, new open-access journals, resource constraints) and avoid blanket dismissals; use multiple verification steps rather than a single label.
